messages.author: 74f2e6fef4c447fd
messages.subject: Question about PM10 CONCENTRATIONS IN PIEMONTE example
parts:
Hello folks,

I have worked through the 'PM10 CONCENTRATIONS IN PIEMONTE' example, the one for a space-time model in INLA.  I am wondering why, in this section of the code,...

#-- Define the formula --#
formula <- (logPM10 ~ -1 + Intercept + A + UTMX + UTMY + WS + TEMP + HMIX + PREC + EMI + 
  f(field, model=spde, group=field.group, control.group=list(model="ar1")))

#-- Call INLA and get results --#
mod.mode =
  inla(formula,
       data=inla.stack.data(stack.est, spde=spde),
       family="gaussian",
       control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.est), compute=FALSE),
       control.compute=list(cpo=FALSE),
       keep=FALSE, verbose=TRUE,
       control.inla=list(reordering="metis"))

...the X and Y coordinates appear to be specified as linear fixed effects.  Is this necessary to have these in the fixed effects part of the formula?  On the other hand, time is not included in the fixed effects part of the formula.  Can you explain for me why space and time are treated differently?  On the other hand, I see that both space and time are dealt with in f().

Thank you for the great set of tools!

Tim

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about PM10 CONCENTRATIONS IN PIEMONTE example
parts:
On 28 Jul 2015, at 06:04, TDM <tme...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have worked through the 'PM10 CONCENTRATIONS IN PIEMONTE' example, the one for a space-time model in INLA.  I am wondering why, in this section of the code,...

...the X and Y coordinates appear to be specified as linear fixed effects.  Is this necessary to have these in the fixed effects part of the formula?  On the other hand, time is not included in the fixed effects part of the formula.  Can you explain for me why space and time are treated differently?  On the other hand, I see that both space and time are dealt with in f().

Hi,
There is no reason one couldn't also add a linear temporal trend to the model, but if I recall correctly the data ever didn't exhibit a temporal trend, or there wasn't enough data to infer one.

The main reason that space and time are treated differently is simply that space and time here behave very differently; the spatial covariates capture systematic effects due to geographical effects. There is no reason for that to be linear in longitude and/or latitude, but it helps to capture large scale effects with large scale spatial covariates so that the space-time SPDE can "focus" on non-systematic, local, and more random effects, instead of having to also capture all of the persistent geographical effects.
Thank you for the great set of tools!

Thanks!

Finn


Tim
